newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: FORECAST - Poll sees Singapore '96 growth at 7.1 pct.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Poll sees Singapore '96 growth at 7.1 pct.

text.p: Economists have cut their forecasts for growth of the Singapore economy this year by one full percentage point to 7.1 percent year-on-year, a Reuters poll of leading financial institutions showed on Wednesday.

The poll of 11 economists was carried out on Wednesday morning after the release on Tuesday of the figures for Singapore's industrial production in July and U.S. semiconductor order book data for August.
Most of those polled said they had cut their forecasts over the last few weeks to reflect the impact on the economy of the slowdown in the U.S. electronics industry.

Electronics and related products account for around half Singapore's industrial production and some 60 percent of its non-oil exports. As a result, Singapore's economy tends to follow closely the performance of the U.S. electronics industry.

Forecasts for growth for the third quarter of the year have shown the sharpest downward revisions, producing an average estimate of 4.9 percent growth year-on-year, compared with 9.8 percent in the third quarter of 1995.
The Singapore economy is expected to expand by 6.1 percent in the fourth quarter, compared with 9.1 percent in the last three months of 1995, the poll showed.
The economy expanded by seven percent in the second quarter after growing 10.9 percent in the first quarter.
The government has said it expects the economy to grow by between seven and eight percent in 1996.
Singapore's Economic Development Board said on Tuesday the city-state's total manufacturing output grew 1.3 percent in July year-on-year after falling 1.3 percent in June.

The U.S. Semiconductor Industry Association said overnight its so called book-to-bill ratio, which measures new orders of the electronic components against shipments, had risen to 0.90 in August from a revised 0.86 in July.
A figure below 1.00 in the book-to-bill ratio indicates demand for computer chips is slowing.

Economists and analysts in Singapore said the two sets of data had confirmed their fairly bearish view of the electronics sector and the Singapore manufacturing sector in general for the next six months.

They were heartened by the small rise in the U.S. book-to-bill ratio but noted that the ratio was still negative and that new orders for U.S. computer chips were down 37.8 percent in August year-on-year.
The U.S. book-to-bill ratio is generally regarded as a key leading indicator for Singapore, with changes in the U.S. data showing up about six months later in the Singapore economy.
Singapore is expected to publish its official figures for third quarter economic growth in mid-November.
